I do still use those when I want something rich that it looks like you could just fall into. Like a rich black from crimson alizarin and pthalo green, incredible stuff for something like a night sky. But if you use that, you can't mix it with anything except another alizarin or pthalo because you lose the depths of color (the rich, deep colors are caused by the pigments being made from clay and clay-like substances that have a thin, wafer structure). But the pthalos and alizarins are how you do glaze layers - a little at a time, lightly applied, come back in a few days apply another layer. It gives it a richness and depth you just can't get any other way and is a lot like some of the classical masters and some of the "newer ones" like Rothko.

As for fugitive issues, have you tried sealing your painting with a UV protectant, then damar and then again with gamar (yes, gamar, not damar)? The damar bonds to the surface, the gamar does not. So the damar provides an actual bonded surface to protect it while the gamar on top can be removed if it gets scuffed, splattered, etc. Check this link and look for the section called "notes on Varnish": http://www.peterdiianni.com/writings/preserving-artwork.html

One of the great things about impressionists is that they relied on partitive color... that is that they didn't always blend their colors on the palette but let them mix in your eye. By putting those colors in small amounts next to each other, our brain and eyes can't really see the minute details and it mixes in our eyes. Impressionists also used each color all over the canvas, creating a sense of unity. You could try either introducing some colors into the black areas, maybe glazed on top (you'll need to thin with oil, likely linseed or whatever you're using in your mix) or you can try to introduce that black in other parts of the painting (again, thinned and glazed) to tie those areas together so that the contrast between your other areas and this deep black isn't so stark.

You could also try using the base colors used in your black more throughout the painting. For example, if you're using ultramarine and burnt umber, try using those a little more in other areas. Again, what you're looking for is unity but in this case, you're using the primary components in a way that pulls the eye away from your black and creates a sense of grounding. If your black is "good enough," the viewer's eye will return to it on its own and then get pulled away back to those other areas and create a sense of movement and interest. Of course, the other technique will do this as well but this one is a bit more subtle. But since there rare few things with those kinds of "pure" colors in the world, this method is trickier. It's easier to put shadows in other areas then it is to put believable colors everywhere.
